restatements.text: Allows parents of children eligible for public school to open an education savings account, into which the state must deposit 90% of the per-pupil funding the child's resident district would otherwise receive.
Permits the funds in these accounts to be spent on private school tuition, tutoring, textbooks, and approved online courses.

analysis.answer: Compared to current law, which restricts state education funds to public school districts and charter schools, the measure allows parents to open an education savings account and receive 90% of the state per-pupil funding their child's district would have received, to be used for private educational expenses.

The direct cost is the transfer of 90% of per-pupil funding to the education savings accounts. If eligible students who currently attend private school (without state funding) enroll in the program, this would represent a new net cost to the state budget.

Parents who utilize the accounts and private educational service providers (private schools, tutors) benefit from the funding. Public school districts bear the cost of losing per-pupil funding when students opt out, though they also have fewer students to educate.

More families may transition from public to private education or homeschooling. Public school districts may have to reduce budgets or consolidate if enrollment drops. Private schools and tutors may see increased demand and could potentially increase their tuition or fees.

The measure addresses a lack of public funding for alternative education options by empowering parents to direct state funds toward private education. It may create challenges for public school districts, which have fixed costs that do not decrease proportionally when individual students leave, potentially straining their remaining resources.
Parents gain discretion over how state educational funds are allocated for their children. Private schools, tutoring companies, and educational vendors gain a new source of state-funded revenue.

Researchers disagree on the long-term effects of education savings accounts and vouchers. Some studies find they improve student outcomes through competition and by matching students to preferred schools, while others find they can negatively impact public school finances and lead to worse academic outcomes for students who transfer or remain in public schools.

flags.note: The text does not specify which entity approves the courses or the criteria for approval, leaving it to future implementation by an agency or board.

items.text: Expands education options beyond assigned public schools by funding private tuition and tutoring.
Increases parents' authority to direct state funds for their children's education.
Decreases resources for public school districts when students use the accounts.

Retains state per-pupil funding for district public schools without diverting it to individual accounts.

Forgoes giving parents direct control over state educational funds for their children.
